title: Sun Tzu Drills the King's Concubines
text:
Sima Qian tells how Sun Wu, known as Sun Tzu, a native of Qi, came to King Helu of Wu with his thirteen chapters on the art of war. The king said he had read them all and asked whether Sun Wu could give a small test of his methods, using women. Sun Wu agreed.

One hundred and eighty women from the palace were brought out. Sun Wu divided them into two companies, put one of the king's two favorite concubines at the head of each, and gave everyone a halberd. He explained the commands carefully: front, back, left and right, signaled by the drum. Then he gave the order to face right. The women burst out laughing.

Sun Wu said that if the orders are not clear, it is the general's fault. He explained them again, several times, and gave the order to face left. Again they laughed. Now, he said, the orders were clear, and if they were not carried out, it was the fault of the officers. He ordered the two captains beheaded. The king, watching from a terrace, sent word begging him to spare them. Sun Wu replied that a general in command does not accept every order of his ruler, and had them executed.

He appointed the next women as captains. This time the drill was carried out perfectly, in silence. The king made him a general.
lesson: Make your expectations unmistakably clear first. Then enforce them consistently, including for people close to power, or the rules mean nothing.
people: Sun Wu (Sun Tzu), King Helu of Wu
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 65
caveat: Many historians doubt this story, and even whether Sun Wu existed as Sima Qian describes him.
